findings.body: owner_id is interpolated directly into the SQL string via an f-string, allowing an attacker to inject arbitrary SQL. The separate cursor.execute(query) line on the next line should be removed.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes owner_id = "'; DROP TABLE orders; --" which is interpolated into the query string, executing arbitrary SQL against the database.
findings.title: Use a parameterized query to prevent SQL injection

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The default events=[] is a single list object shared across all calls that omit the argument. Each call appends to the same list, so every subsequent call returns all previously recorded events and the list grows unboundedly. Use events: list[str] | None = None and initialize a new list inside the function when events is None.
findings.failure_scenario: First call register_shipment_events("A") returns {"A": ["A"]}; second call register_shipment_events("B") returns {"B": ["A", "B"]} because both calls mutate the same default list.
findings.title: Replace mutable default argument with None

findings.body: The function accepts `threshold: float` and its docstring says rows are flagged when their total "crosses the review threshold", but the comparison hardcodes `5000` and never reads `threshold`. The parameter is dead, so the function does not honor the caller's threshold.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes `flag_large_backorder_totals(rows, threshold=1000)` expecting rows with total > 1000 to be flagged; the function instead flags only rows with total > 5000, so rows in (1000, 5000] are silently omitted and the returned set does not reflect the requested threshold.
findings.title: Use the `threshold` parameter instead of hardcoded 5000

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12 (it emits a DeprecationWarning) and returns a naive datetime. The modern replacement is datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc), which returns a timezone-aware value. The file already does `import datetime`, so datetime.timezone resolves correctly.
findings.failure_scenario: The naive UTC timestamp written to created_at is later compared against a timezone-aware datetime, and Python raises TypeError instead of completing the comparison.
findings.title: Use timezone-aware datetime.now()

findings.anchor: def flag_large_backorder_totals(rows: list[dict[str, object]], threshold: float) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
findings.body: The `threshold` parameter is accepted but never used — the comparison hardcodes `5000`. This is premature configurability: the parameter exists to look configurable but does nothing. Callers who pass a different threshold get silently ignored. Use the parameter, and the whole body collapses to a list comprehension.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `threshold=1000` expecting rows with total > 1000 to be flagged, but the function still uses the hardcoded 5000, so rows with total between 1000 and 5000 are silently not flagged.
findings.title: Use the threshold parameter instead of hardcoding 5000

findings.body: The query has no LIMIT and no status filter, yet the docstring says it loads queued rows; fetchall() therefore materializes the customer's entire order history into memory in one call.
findings.failure_scenario: A customer with a large order history causes the function to load every one of those rows at once, inflating memory use and latency on each call.
findings.title: Add a limit or pagination to the order fetch

findings.body: `label in seen` is a linear scan over a list, making the whole function O(n²); a set gives O(1) membership tests while preserving first-seen order via the labels list.
findings.failure_scenario: With many rows, each membership test scans the growing seen list, so total work grows quadratically with the number of rows.

    labels: list[str] = []

findings.title: Hoist the carrier-independent count out of the loop

findings.body: Building a list of (score, entry) tuples, sorting it, then unpacking is exactly what `sorted` with a `key` argument does directly. The five-line body collapses to one expression. Note the loop also starts at index 1, silently dropping the first entry — the one-liner fixes that too.

findings.body: The inner double loop over `zones` and `weights` produces the same count for every carrier, so the triple loop repeats identical work `len(carriers)` times. Compute the count once and build the dict in one expression.

    return {carrier: count for carrier in carriers}
